item.description: The Ediacaran-Cambrian interval marks major environmental change and the emergence of complex life, coinciding with some of the weakest magnetic field strengths in Earth history. It has been proposed that inner core nucleation near this boundary triggered a rapid strengthening of the geodynamo during the early Cambrian, but direct constraints on magnetic field behavior across this interval remain limited. Here, we present new paleointensity results from two Cambrian igneous sequences in Brazil (~525 million years ago) and Nova Scotia (~505 million years ago). Using multiple complementary methods, both records indicate a reversing geomagnetic field that remained weak. Combined with a reanalysis of published data, our results show that weak magnetic field conditions persisted for tens of millions of years after the Cambrian radiation. item.title: Quantifying subsurface fracture damage in glaciers using fiber-optic seismology
item.dc:creator: Thomas S. Hudson

item.description: Crevassing critically controls glacier stability. Crevasses can penetrate deep into a glacier or ice shelf, promoting calving, ice avalanches, and even sudden catastrophic ice shelf collapse. Yet quantifying subsurface fracture damage remains largely unquantified. Here, we show how distributed acoustic sensing technology can quantify subsurface fracture damage in unprecedented detail at an alpine glacier. We first demonstrate that seismic anisotropy can quantify fracture extent. We also study crevasse icequake failure mechanisms, which fail predominantly via tensile opening. Icequake-derived crevasse opening is consistent with anisotropy-derived estimates (∼8% of total ice volume), suggesting that damage is dominated by fracture rather than melt. These results establish a scalable approach for monitoring subsurface ice damage that complements existing satellite surface observations. Applications range from monitoring the stability of alpine glaciers that pose a risk to alpine communities to providing foundations for assessing subsurface fracture extent at globally pertinent ice sheets and ice shelves. item.description: Abstract Phosphite and pyrophosphate—reduced and polymerized forms of phosphorus—may have played a central role in prebiotic chemistry owing to their higher reactivity and solubility, yet their geological sources remain uncertain. Here we show that mafic–ultramafic rocks on the early Earth could have provided a sustained source of reactive phosphorus through seafloor weathering. Rock analyses from 15 localities reveal phosphite comprising up to 7%, 24%, 17%, and 0.6% of total phosphorus in olivine separates, peridotite, komatiite, and basalt, respectively, while pyrophosphate accounts for up to 5% and 0.4% in komatiite and basalt. Box-model calculations indicate phosphite concentrations reaching up to 1 µM in the deep ocean and up to 67 µM in lakes under low-UV conditions. We suggest that reactive phosphorus released from mafic–ultramafic rocks could have fuelled prebiotic phosphorylation and supplied phosphate to emerging life on Earth, a process that may also enhance the habitability of other planetary bodies. item.title: U.S. rivers are transporting more suspended sediment, often in less time
item.dc:creator: Nishchal Sigdel
Admin Husic
item.description: Abstract Riverine suspended sediment transport is highly episodic, yet how the timing and magnitude of these bursts have shifted under climate and land-use change remains uncertain. Here, we integrate high-frequency turbidity sensing with deep learning to reconstruct nearly four decades of daily sediment flux for 175 U.S. rivers. We apply a temporal inequality framework to quantify multi-decadal trends in sediment timing alongside magnitude. Annual sediment yields have risen at 28% of rivers and export has become time-compressed at 33% of rivers, with the network-wide median days required to deliver 90% of the annual load dropping from 69 in 1985 to 50 in 2023. These trends in magnitude and timing are partially decoupled, as only 15% of sites show both, and they are governed by distinct attributed drivers. Land-use change is the dominant predictor of temporal compression, while intensifying precipitation is the dominant predictor of rising sediment yields. Both trends are most pronounced in small, urbanizing catchments. The result is a narrowing window for monitoring and intervention, complicating downstream sediment management and water-quality operations. item.description: The contributions of mantle plumes to the formation of magmatic nickel–copper–platinum-group element sulfide deposits remain poorly characterized. Here, we assess this ambiguity by utilizing the Hg isotope composition of sulfide ores from the giant Jinchuan deposit and those within the Central Asian Orogenic Belt, which represent magmatic sulfide deposits that formed within intracratonic and orogenic settings, respectively. The Δ^199Hg values of the sulfide ores within the Central Asian Orogenic Belt (0.01 ± 0.16‰, 2 SD) and Jinchuan (−0.03 ± 0.11‰, 2 SD) are similar to those of mantle plumes (0.0 ± 0.1‰, 2 SD), but distinctly different from those of metasomatized lithospheric mantle (non-zero). This supports a plume origin for magmatic sulfide deposit formation, regardless of their formation in intracratonic or orogenic settings. These findings help to better understand the genesis of magmatic sulfide deposits in a diversity of tectonic settings and provide new insights into Hg isotope behavior during magmatic sulfide mineralization. Δ199Hg values in Central Asian Orogenic Belt and Jinchuan sulfide ores match mantle plume signatures and differ from metasomatized lithospheric mantle, indicating a mantle plume origin for these deposits, according to Hg isotope analysis of the Ni–Cu PGE ore samples. item.title: Radial gradient of superionic hydrogen in the Earth’s inner core
item.dc:creator: Zepeng Wu
Liangrui Wei

Shunqing Wu

item.prism:publicationName: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
item.description: Hydrogen is considered a key light element in Earth’s core, yet the thermodynamics of its superionic phase and its distribution in the inner core remain unclear. Here, we compute ab initio Gibbs free energies for liquid and superionic hcp and bcc Fe–H phases and construct the superionic–liquid phase diagram over pressure–temperature conditions relevant to the Earth’s inner core. We find that phase diagrams at different inner-core pressures collapse when temperatures are scaled by the melting temperature of pure iron, indicating that solid–liquid partitioning is controlled primarily by a reduced temperature relative to iron melting and is weakly sensitive to pressure. This scaling relation further reconciles previously reported discrepancies in partition coefficients among theoretical studies and yields good agreement with available experimental data at low pressures. By applying thermochemical constraints, our free-energy results reveal a radial hydrogen gradient within the inner core. These results demonstrate that compositional gradients of superionic hydrogen in the inner core emerge naturally from equilibrium thermodynamics and suggest a general mechanism governing the depth-dependent distribution of light elements within Earth’s inner core. item.title: Widespread tropical cyclone activity during the Late Paleozoic Ice Age
item.dc:creator: Qing Yan
Sophia Macarewich

item.description: A combination of high-resolution (~25-km) simulations and storm deposits point to widespread tropical cyclone activity during the Late Paleozoic Ice Age and a poleward shift in response to CO_2-induced glacial-interglacial transitions. Whether tropical cyclone (TC) activity prevailed during the Late Paleozoic Ice Age (LPIA)—the longest icehouse of the Phanerozoic—remains debated, owing to the paucity and ambiguity of sedimentary evidence. To help resolve this conflict, we combine a global compilation of 126 storm records spanning the LPIA ( ~ 360–260 Ma) with high-resolution (~25-km) TC-resolving simulations. We reveal a quasi-symmetric meridional distribution of TC genesis across the tropics during the LPIA, with TC tracks extending into high latitudes (>60°N/°S). This pattern aligns with the compiled widespread storm deposits from subtropical and tropical regions. During CO₂-driven glacial–interglacial transitions within the LPIA, we observe reduced global TC frequency and enhanced intensity, coinciding with poleward shifts in TC activity. The shifts are linked to spatially heterogeneous warming patterns and associated changes in atmospheric circulation. Our results help reconcile controversies regarding icehouse TC behavior and highlight that warming-induced poleward migration of TC activity is likely a climate state-independent characteristic of the Earth system. item.dc:creator: Luuk van Agtmaal

item.description: Abstract Plate corners in collisional orogens are often characterized by sharply curved orogenic zones, that is, orogenic syntaxis zones, where tectonic mountain building and surface processes vigorously interact. The formation and evolution of syntaxis zones, which are particularly well expressed in the eastern and western terminations of the Himalayan orogen, remain debated. Here, based on 3D thermomechanical surface process numerical experiments, we propose that the formation of the Eastern Himalayan syntaxis is predominantly driven by flattening of the Indian slab and shear localization in the weak Eurasian crust. Our models indicate that a northward migrating syntaxis initially forms during collision with India when the middle to lower crust in the Eurasian plate is rheologically weak beneath a proto-plateau. This syntaxis becomes a barrier for the laterally expanding plateau. The corner of the collision zone is dismembered by the localization of crustal-scale strike–slip fault zones driven by slab flattening and differential plate advance. The middle to lower crust locally flows within a narrow channel from the plateau towards the east and south along the syntaxis. These links between slab dynamics and crustal shear localization drive the structural and topographic evolution of orogenic syntaxis. item.description: Pegmatites of the lithium-cesium-tantalum type are widely dismissed as potential scandium hosts. Here we show that beryl from the Bailongshan pegmatite deposit in northwest China contains anomalously high scandium, with scandium oxide reaching up to 1.85 wt%, and present direct nanoscale evidence of dislocation-mediated critical metal enrichment in beryl. Scandium-rich beryl-bearing pegmatites form a distinct metallogenic subunit hosted in scandium-rich two-mica schists. Beryl crystals have a magmatic core surrounded by a hydrothermal rim; despite continuous crystal structure, the rim holds nearly twice the scandium content of the adjacent dislocation-free core. Dislocation arrays in the rim create fast-diffusion pathways and expand atomic sites to accommodate scandium leached from wall rocks by hydrothermal fluids, with whole-rock grades corresponding to an estimated 7.4–12.0 kiloton scandium resource. This post-crystallization, dislocation-driven mechanism operates independently of magmatic fractionation, redefining such pegmatites intruding scandium-rich metasedimentary rocks as underexplored global scandium resources. Hydrothermal alteration generated dislocations in beryl rims that facilitated Sc diffusion and enrichment, leading to significant scandium accumulation and highlighting the Bailongshan deposit in Northwest China as a promising Sc resource, according to geochemical and crystallographic analysis. item.title: Punctuated garnet growth within a protracted zircon record distinguishes reaction dates from residence times in North Qaidam eclogites
item.dc:creator: Kai-Yang Du

item.description: Constraining the duration of (ultra)high-pressure metamorphism is central to quantifying rates of continental subduction and exhumation, yet the answer depends on which mineral is dated. Zircon U-Pb date spectra are routinely read as residence times, but zircon may grow, dissolve, and recrystallize across many stages of a pressure–temperature path, whereas garnet records the discrete reactions that produced it. We combine microsampled garnet Lu-Hf and Sm-Nd geochronology, zircon U-Pb dating, trace-element systematics, phase-equilibrium modeling, and a quantitative modal rare-earth-element (REE) budget for eclogites from the Dulan area of the North Qaidam terrane. Garnet core and rim fractions from three samples yield indistinguishable Lu-Hf dates ranging from 439.1 ± 1.8 to 442.5 ± 1.9 Ma, recording garnet growth within analytical resolution at ∼2.6–3.0 GPa and 660–720 °C. Pseudosection modeling links this garnet growth to a single overstepped dehydration reaction releasing ∼1.6 wt% water. Zircon dates, by contrast, span ca. 484–427 Ma, and zircon trace-element and Ti-in-zircon systematics evolve systematically through this interval, indicating growth and modification across multiple stages rather than continuous eclogite-facies residence. Modal REE budget calculations show that flat heavy-REE patterns are non-unique, as retrograde amphibole and epidote or zoisite can reproduce an eclogite-like signature. These results demonstrate that garnet and zircon monitor fundamentally distinct processes: a discrete reaction pulse versus an integrated history. Their divergence, not their agreement, is diagnostic of metamorphic evolution. Comparison with other large (U)HP terranes shows that apparent multi-million-year “protracted” (U)HP spectra can readily emerge from short, single-rock garnet pulses combined with diachronous burial and exhumation of tectonic slices. Accessory-mineral-only chronologies may therefore conflate distinct reactions with prolonged residence. Mineral dates in (U)HP terranes must first be read as reaction dates, using growth-pulse geochronology, zircon compositional and thermometric trends, and modal REE budgets, before they can be converted into residence-time estimates. item.description: Epizonal orogenic gold systems in shallow metamorphic belts commonly exhibit contrasting styles of antimony (Sb)-rich and Sb-poor mineralization, yet the controlling factors remain debated. Here, we integrate vein classifications with fluid inclusion microthermometry and oxygen isotope data from the giant Zaozigou Au-Sb deposit (West Qinling, China) to constrain the pressure-temperature (P-T) conditions and fluid evolution. Our results demonstrate that differential stress (σ1 − σ3) governs the spatial segregation of Sb-rich and Sb-poor mineralization through its control on failure modes and fluid processes. Two distinct orebody types are identified: (1) steeply dipping Au orebodies (60°−90°) with subeconomic Sb grades (<1 wt%), hosted in shear fractures and dominated by disseminated arsenopyrite and pyrite with invisible Au; and (2) gently dipping Au-Sb orebodies (19°−45°) with high Sb grades (average 5 wt%), characterized by native gold-bearing stibnite-quartz veins in extension fractures. Fluid inclusion data reveal that steeply dipping orebodies formed under stable P-T conditions (∼0.8 kbar, ∼250 °C), whereas gently dipping orebodies experienced significant decompression (∼1.1 kbar to ∼0.4 kbar) and cooling (∼250 °C to ∼190 °C). Our comprehensive analysis demonstrates that steeply dipping orebodies formed through shear failure of intact rock under high differential stress conditions (σ1 − σ3 ≥ 5.7T) and subsequent fault reactivation under decreased differential stress conditions related to seismic stress release, with gold precipitation dominated by fluid-rock interaction. In contrast, gently dipping orebodies developed in intact rock under low differential stress (σ1 − σ3 < 4T), where fluid immiscibility triggered H2S degassing and rapid Au-Sb deposition. The mechanical relationships observed at Zaozigou may provide new insights into the enrichment of Sb in shallow epizonal orogenic gold deposits. The systematic decrease of differential stress with reduced depth in brittle regimes creates conditions favorable for Sb mineralization at upper crustal levels, where lower stress environments promote extensional failure and the substantial pressure fluctuations required for efficient Sb deposition. This stress-based framework offers a potential explanation for the characteristic vertical zoning of Sb in orogenic systems, complementing existing genetic models. item.description: The Candle Lake C29/30 kimberlite, erupted on the northwestern Sask Craton, Canada, contains diamonds of both lithospheric and sublithospheric origin. The lithospheric diamonds are relatively large, often highly resorbed and nitrogen-rich, and derive from eclogitic substrates, as indicated by their inclusion load and by carbon and nitrogen isotope compositions. Observation of CO2 micro-inclusions in some of these diamonds suggests their formation by oxidized fluids. Their nitrogen aggregation systematics are consistent with a main diamond formation at ∼1.27 Ga at steady geothermal conditions, as reported for diamonds from Fort à La Corne. The sublithospheric diamonds have unusual pristine octahedral shapes, often being aggregates of multiple crystals, are relatively small (0.1 to 1.5 mm) and nitrogen-free. They have carbon isotope compositions close to the mantle value and carry mineral inclusions indicating their formation in carbonated metaperidotitic substrates at deep upper mantle to lower mantle depths. The observation of carbonate inclusions in these diamonds attests to variations in oxygen fugacity conditions during diamond growth. Such an environment may be imposed by a subducted slab equilibrating with the ambient sublithospheric mantle, where diamonds may have formed through carbonate reduction. Our new garnet xenocryst dataset for Candle Lake indicates a lithospheric column dominated by lherzolites, which, in the deeper parts, experienced intense metasomatism by Ti-rich melts. The high abundance of Ti-rich garnets at Candle Lake supports the previously proposed connection between such garnets and the presence of sublithospheric diamonds; Ti-metasomatism may have also caused resorption of the lithospheric diamonds before the accretion of sublithospheric diamonds. item.description: The role of reduced sulfur in tungsten (W) transport and precipitation is a critical issue in the genesis of hydrothermal tungsten deposits. The Shangfang tungsten deposit in southeastern China is hosted in mafic rocks that well preserve the geochemical signatures of the original reduced ore-forming fluid and mineralization. This study integrates in situ sulfur isotope and trace-element data from sulfides (pyrrhotite, pyrite, chalcopyrite), and thermodynamic modeling to elucidate the reduced-sulfur-driven mineralization mechanism. Sulfur isotope fractionation between pyrite-pyrrhotite pairs constrains the main mineralization temperature to 240-350°C. In situ sulfur isotope compositions and trace-element data of sulfide also confirm that the dominant sulfur and tungsten sources are of magmatic-hydrothermal origin. Thermodynamic modeling of alteration mineralogy and sulfur isotopes demonstrates that a physicochemical environment falls within the stability field of thiotungstate complexes (WOnS4-n 2−, n = 0–4). Sulfur-rich, reducing hydrothermal fluids drove the conversion of tungstate to thiotungstate species, which significantly increased tungsten solubility. Widespread intergrowth of scheelite and sulfides in high-grade ores further verifies that reduced sulfur facilitates tungsten migration via thiotungstate species. Water-rock interaction (chloritization and sericitization) promotes the coeval precipitation of scheelite and sulfide. This study demonstrates the decisive role of reduced sulfur in mafic-rock-hosted tungsten systems, which regulates tungsten speciation, improves transport efficiency, and controls tungsten mineralization. item.description: Zircon, typically resistant to hydrothermal alteration, can be significantly modified in fluid-active systems via coupled dissolution–reprecipitation, especially in alkali-rich environments. SEM and CL imaging revealed distinct textures: ZM-14 formed inward-convex fronts and overgrowths, while ZM-5 developed porous, jagged rims. LA-ICP-MS mapping shows systematic trace-element redistribution: altered rims in both natural and experimental zircons are depleted in U (7078–2930 ppm) and Th (764–247 ppm), with cores enriched in Hf (19,344 ppm), Y (5308 ppm), and ΣREE (3841 ppm). Th/U ratios (0.16–0.54) and elevated Yb/Gd (12.9–24.9) indicate K+-mediated fractionation. Experimental overgrowths lack inclusions (vs. PA-1), suggesting kinetic limitations from Th availability or reaction duration. item.dc:creator: Sophia E. Economon

item.description: Abstract Planetary volatiles cycle through a planet's crust, mantle, and atmosphere, playing a crucial role in surface processes and habitability. Discussions of planetary volatiles traditionally focus on water, carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur, but fluids in contact with silicate rocks and ultramafic mantles can contain significant amounts of magnesium and silicon. Ultramafic mantles may be common in our solar system and can be expected in many exoplanets. These environments have been studied through fluid inclusions in diamonds from Earth's upper mantle and in experiments of chloride‐free fluids in equilibrium with peridotite. It appears that magnesium‐chloride complexing is increasingly relevant at high temperatures and pressures, but such complexes are largely unconstrained for deep conditions. Effective models are needed to understanding volatile cycling on terrestrial worlds in our solar system and beyond. To address this, we analyzed published experimental data for silicate mineral solubilities in chloride‐rich fluids to assess fluid speciation in ultramafic planetary mantles. We regressed experimental solubilities of talc + quartz and tremolite + talc + quartz at 2 kb and 500–700°C, as well as solubilities of forsterite at 10 kb and 800–900°C to obtain new equilibrium constants for and revised equilibrium constants for several magnesium‐, calcium‐, and silicon‐bearing species. We then applied the DEW model to characterize the equilibrium constants over wide ranges of temperature and pressure. As a result, we produce a new and robust thermodynamic data set for magnesium‐, calcium‐, and silicon‐chloride complexes at upper mantle conditions which enable modeling of magnesium transport in deep planetary fluids. item.description: The Qukulekedong AuSb deposit, located in the western East Kunlun Orogenic Belt, contains resources of 21.5 t Au and 73 kt Sb and has been interpreted as an intrusion-related AuSb system. item.description: The Youjiang Basin in South China, a part of the Paleo-Tethys Ocean, hosts significant carbonate-hosted sedimentary manganese (Mn) resources, characterized by stratigraphically confined, intense, and episodic mineralization from the Devonian to Triassic, linked closely to palaeogeographic evolution of the basin driven by episodic tectonic events. This review synthesizes the palaeogeographic evolution of the Youjiang Basin, the spatiotemporal distribution as well as the mineralogical, sedimentological, geochemical, and geochronological constraints on Youjiang Mn deposits, gaining several key insights: (1) Basin tectonics, driven by rifting, subduction, and back-arc volcanisms, formed fault-segmented basin-platform systems, regulating Mn supply, redox-stratified water columns, and sediment-starved depositional settings; (2) Mn mineralization occurred episodically, with Devonian–Early Carboniferous deposits forming in deep-water, low-clastic-input settings through redoxcline-controlled sequestration of Mn(III/IV) (oxyhydr)oxide precursors and their reduction to Mn-rich carbonates by organic matter during the diagenesis stage, whereas Permian-Triassic deposits reflect stratigraphically persistent Mn-enriched layers influenced by glacio-eustatic cycles, post-extinction redox instability, and low dilution; (3) Hydrothermal fluids and syndepositional faulting were primary Mn sources, with Mn(II) accumulating in anoxic deep waters and/or pore waters and being fixed near redoxcline conditions through microbial and redox-mediated oxidation processes; (4) Organic matter participation and microbially mediated diagenesis jointly facilitated stable Mn carbonate precipitation under high-alkalinity marine conditions. We hereby establish a comprehensive genetic metallogenic model, highlighting dynamic couplings among tectonically controlled Mn supply, stratified redox conditions, sea-level-driven redoxcline migration, microbial Mn cycling, and early diagenetic carbonate fixation, with mineralization occurring during periods of enhanced Mn flux, sustained stratification, efficient Mn sequestration, and low dilution. This review synthesis advances fundamental cognition of sedimentary manganese metallogeny and supports sustainable exploration and exploitation of Mn resources in the Youjiang Basin. item.description: The impact of the northward subduction of the Meso-Tethys Ocean (Bangong-Nujiang Tethyan Ocean) on the tectonic-sedimentary evolution of the South Qiangtang terrane remains poorly constrained. item.description: Abstract Two types of crystallised melt were identified as tiny, sharply bounded, ellipsoidal inclusions (typically 20–80 µm) in metamorphosed massive pyrrhotite ore (12–14 kbar, ~530–550 °C) from the VMS Besshi-type Tisová deposit. item.description: The magmatic-hydrothermal transition in rare-metal pegmatites is crucial for understanding mineralizing processes, particularly for strategic resources like lithium and beryllium. Tourmaline, a common mineral in pegmatites, serves as an excellent geochemical tracer for this transition. This study examines the Bailongshan Li pegmatite deposit in the western Kunlun Orogen, northwestern China, through detailed textural and geochemical analyses of elbaite (Elb). By integrating data for major and trace elements and Li–B isotope compositions of Elb, the present study delineates the magmatic-hydrothermal transition and its role in ore formation. item.description: Horizontal hydraulic opening-mode fractures are widely developed across sedimentary, magmatic, and metamorphic crustal environments. For the general case where the vertical stress corresponds to the lithostatic load, such fracturing is favored under compressive stress regimes at low differential stress, when the fluid pressures exceeding the lithostatic load (i.e., achieving super-lithostatic fluid overpressures). In many cases these fractures contain blocky mineral fills, indicating that deposition occurred within an open, fluid-filled space owing to a lack of spanning during opening. Some evidence from primary fluid inclusions within these blocky cements, along with some conceptual interpretation from all three crustal systems, demonstrate that super-lithostatic fluid overpressures could also be present during syn-kinematic blocky cementations within these fractures, which provided the potential for maintaining them open against the lithostatic load and accommodating blocky crystallization. However, the mechanical significance of such fluid-pressure–tectonic coupling, particularly the role of super-lithostatic fluid overpressure in sustaining horizontal fractures open and blocky cementation have not yet been systematically synthesized across crustal environments. In this review, we focus on the scenarios where super-lithostatic fluid overpressure does occur, and its coupling with tectonic stresses to facilitate horizontal hydraulic opening-mode fracturing and blocky cementation in the crust. Some case studies across diverse systems demonstrate that super-lithostatic fluid overpressures—generated via gas generation during thermal cracking in sedimentary shales, volatile exsolution within intrusion roof zones in magmatic systems (e.g., porphyry-epithermal ore deposit, granite-related Sn-W deposit and pegmatite), or devolatilization reactions in metamorphic orogenic gold belts—consistently coupled with compressive regimes to drive horizontal hydraulic fracturing and sustain open spaces for blocky deposition. Taken together, this synthesis highlights that super-lithostatic fluid overpressure plays a pivotal dual role in both forming horizontal opening-mode fracturing and mechanically maintaining the open spaces required for subsequent blocky cementation, a mechanism that directly controls crustal fluid focusing and mineral accumulation, particularly for sedimentary hydrocarbons, orogenic precious metals, and magmatic critical minerals. item.description: The Jiangnan Orogen (JO) is widely acknowledged as the suture zone between the Yangtze and Cathaysia Blocks in South China, yet the precise timing of their collision remains a subject of ongoing debate. item.description: Silicification is typically volumetrically minor in carbonate successions, but is critical for paleoenvironmental reconstruction, paleobiology, and reservoir characterization because chert preserves primary features and records key depositional, stratigraphic, diagenetic, and hydrothermal events. In continental carbonates, however, silicification remains underexplored and is commonly treated within isolated depositional or diagenetic contexts. This review integrates silicification styles across continental carbonate environments and proposes a unifying framework linking silica macrotextures to chemical and hydrologic conditions and silica sources. The framework establishes a continuum from displacive nodular fabrics in pedogenic and palustrine settings to stratiform cherts in phreatic and lacustrine systems, and ultimately to chemically precipitated silica in extreme alkaline lakes. The framework is explored using the Aptian South Atlantic Pre-Salt lacustrine succession, particularly the Barra Velha Formation (Santos Basin), as an example of large-scale continental silicification. The Pre-Salt displays distinctive intra-bed silicification patterns driven by multiple internal silica sources, efficient recycling, and strong geochemical competition among carbonate, Mg-clay minerals, and silica phases, forming one of the largest documented continental silica sinks. Stratabound replacement of Mg-clay–rich facies predominates, consistent with predictions from a pH–silica activity model and indicative of alkaline lacustrine conditions. Early precipitation of multiple silica phases, including hydrated precursors, complicates microfabric interpretation following burial and diagenetic overprint. Although volumetrically limited, early silicification significantly influences reservoir quality by controlling diagenetic evolution and enhancing horizontal permeability in fractured silicified intervals. This review provides an integrated framework for understanding continental carbonate silicification, silica cycling, microfabric development, and reservoir heterogeneity in ancient alkaline lake systems. item.description: High-sulfidation epithermal deposits, typically formed at shallow crustal levels (<1.5 km), are highly vulnerable to erosion, making their preservation and final exposure level largely dependent on the post-mineralization exhumation history. The Zijinshan Cu-Au deposit in southeastern China is a world-class high-sulfidation system, yet its post-mineralization cooling and exhumation pathway remain poorly constrained, hindering a full understanding of its preservation mechanism and regional implications. This study presents the first coupled zircon (ZHe) and apatite (AHe) (U-Th)/He thermochronologic investigation on Zijinshan, utilizing samples from a ∼1300 m vertical profile within the hydrothermally altered granitic host rock. ZHe ages range from 106.8 ± 5.6 Ma to 65.3 ± 3.7 Ma, showing a general positive correlation with elevation, while AHe ages from one sample range from 55.1 ± 3.1 Ma to 22.4 ± 1.3 Ma. Inverse thermal history modeling, constrained by these data, reveals a five-stage cooling history since ∼115 Ma: (I) terminal magmatic-hydrothermal cooling (100–95 Ma); (II) Late Cretaceous tectonic denudation (83–75 Ma) linked to Paleo-Pacific slab rollback; (III) a prolonged period of tectonic quiescence with slow cooling (75–48 Ma), critical for shallow preservation; (IV) Eocene accelerated exhumation (48–46 Ma) driven by renewed Pacific slab dynamics; and (V) Late Cenozoic slow, monsoon-influenced denudation (46–0 Ma). Quantitative analysis indicates a total post-75 Ma exhumation of ∼1.7 km, with ∼1.1 km occurring during the Late Cretaceous and ∼0.6 km during the Cenozoic. This “punctuated” exhumation history, characterized by alternating rapid exhumation and long-term upper-crustal residence, allowed Zijinshan to avoid deep erosion and facilitated supergene enrichment of the gold cap. The cooling stages correlate with major Mesozoic–Cenozoic geodynamic transitions in Southeast China, underscoring the dominant control of Pacific plate subduction dynamics. Compared to other metallogenic belts in South China, the Wuyi Belt experienced moderate exhumation, providing a favorable setting for preserving Zijinshan-type epithermal systems. This study establishes a robust thermo-tectonic framework for understanding the preservation of Mesozoic ore systems in Southeast China and offers valuable insights for mineral exploration in similar geologic settings. High-sulfidation epithermal deposits, typically formed at shallow crustal levels (<1.5 km), are highly vulnerable to erosion, making their preservation and final exposure level largely dependent on the post-mineralization exhumation history. The Zijinshan Cu-Au deposit in southeastern China is a world-class high-sulfidation system, yet its post-mineralization cooling and exhumation pathway remain poorly constrained, hindering a full understanding of its preservation mechanism and regional implications. This study presents the first coupled zircon (ZHe) and apatite (AHe) (U-Th)/He thermochronologic investigation on Zijinshan, utilizing samples from a ∼1300 m vertical profile within the hydrothermally altered granitic host rock. ZHe ages range from 106.8 ± 5.6 Ma to 65.3 ± 3.7 Ma, showing a general positive correlation with elevation, while AHe ages from one sample range from 55.1 ± 3.1 Ma to 22.4 ± 1.3 Ma. Inverse thermal history modeling, constrained by these data, reveals a five-stage cooling history since ∼115 Ma: (I) terminal magmatic-hydrothermal cooling (100–95 Ma); (II) Late Cretaceous tectonic denudation (83–75 Ma) linked to Paleo-Pacific slab rollback; (III) a prolonged period of tectonic quiescence with slow cooling (75–48 Ma), critical for shallow preservation; (IV) Eocene accelerated exhumation (48–46 Ma) driven by renewed Pacific slab dynamics; and (V) Late Cenozoic slow, monsoon-influenced denudation (46–0 Ma). Quantitative analysis indicates a total post-75 Ma exhumation of ∼1.7 km, with ∼1.1 km occurring during the Late Cretaceous and ∼0.6 km during the Cenozoic. This “punctuated” exhumation history, characterized by alternating rapid exhumation and long-term upper-crustal residence, allowed Zijinshan to avoid deep erosion and facilitated supergene enrichment of the gold cap. The cooling stages correlate with major Mesozoic–Cenozoic geodynamic transitions in Southeast China, underscoring the dominant control of Pacific plate subduction dynamics. Compared to other metallogenic belts in South China, the Wuyi Belt experienced moderate exhumation, providing a favorable setting for preserving Zijinshan-type epithermal systems. This study establishes a robust thermo-tectonic framework for understanding the preservation of Mesozoic ore systems in Southeast China and offers valuable insights for mineral exploration in similar geologic settings.
